title: Turn a Request into a Testable Task
summary: Clarify who needs a feature, what information it uses, and how you will know it works before choosing a tool.
prerequisites: No previous CRM or Salesforce experience is required.
learningObjectives: Describe a requirement in terms of people and outcomes.
Separate scope, assumptions, and implementation choices.
Write acceptance criteria for valid and invalid cases.

sections.heading: A short request contains unanswered decisions
body: Oleg asks, 'Please add test-drive booking to Salesforce.' This expresses a useful direction, but it is not yet a complete task. Who makes the booking? What information is required? What does booking mean: recording a request, reserving a vehicle, or confirming a customer appointment? These choices affect the data, permissions, and behaviour that the team will eventually build.

Start with the people. Anna needs to record the vehicle and time agreed with Irina so that Max can host the appointment when Anna is away. Anna is the user of this proposed function; Irina is the customer receiving the service. The request does not imply that Irina needs a Salesforce login. Separating the person using the screen from the person affected by the business outcome prevents an unnecessary external portal.

callouts.text: A useful requirement explains the person, the needed outcome, and why it matters.

sections.heading: Ask questions in a workable order
body: First identify the information. Does the vehicle already exist in the catalogue? How is the customer identified? Which time zone does the team use? Then identify the actions: can Anna create, change, confirm, and cancel the appointment? Finally investigate exceptional situations: a vehicle becomes unavailable, a time is already occupied, or Irina changes her mind.

Do not quietly invent answers. Write unknowns as questions and proposals as proposals. Oleg might decide that the first version simply records an appointment after a salesperson checks availability manually. Automatic calendar coordination would then be a later feature. That is a legitimate small scope when it is agreed and described honestly.

Scope is the boundary of the current task. For our first booking feature, an agreed scope might include a vehicle, customer, scheduled time, and appointment status. It might exclude payment, vehicle ownership transfer, and automated reminders. Stating the exclusions helps a reviewer understand what the exercise is intended to demonstrate, without pretending those business needs never exist.

callouts.text: Keep an assumptions list next to the task. Give each unresolved decision an owner who can answer it.

sections.heading: Define evidence of success and failure
body: Acceptance criteria are conditions used to decide whether the agreed behaviour has been delivered. 'Make booking easy' is too ambiguous to test on its own. 'Anna selects an existing vehicle and future time, saves the appointment, reopens it, and sees the same values' describes observable actions and results. A reviewer can repeat that scenario.

Also describe an invalid case. For example, propose that an appointment without a vehicle cannot be confirmed, and that the interface explains what is missing. This is a proposed rule until Oleg agrees. Distinguish that requirement from an implementation suggestion such as 'use a validation rule.' The behaviour should be understood before the team chooses the mechanism.

Finally, think about handover. If Max must conduct the appointment, specify how he identifies the relevant record and whether he may edit it. 'The record exists' is not enough if the intended colleague cannot find it. In later lessons you will implement the data and access choices. Today's deliverable is a clear, small task that another person can understand and test.

callouts.text: For each criterion, could two people perform the same steps and agree whether the expected result happened?

steps.title: Rewrite the request
steps.instruction: Name Anna, the information she records, and the business benefit.
steps.expected: The task describes a person and an outcome.

steps.title: Identify uncertainty
steps.instruction: Write questions about required data, time, cancellation, and Max's access.

steps.title: Write two acceptance examples
steps.instruction: Describe one valid booking and one rejected input using explicit expected results.
steps.expected: A reviewer can reproduce both cases without interpreting vague adjectives.

exercise.title: Prepare a booking brief
exercise.brief: Write a one-page brief for Oleg before creating fields or automation.
steps: State the goal and the user.
List required information, three unanswered questions, and the current scope.
Write one successful and one unsuccessful example.
acceptance: Assumptions are visibly different from confirmed requirements.
Acceptance criteria describe behaviour rather than an unexamined technical solution.

knowledgeCheck.question: Can an invented restriction be treated as a requirement?
knowledgeCheck.answer: No. Record it as a proposal and ask the decision-maker to confirm it.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why identify Max in the task?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Because the handover may require access and a way to find the appointment, not merely record creation.

knowledgeCheck.question: What makes an acceptance criterion testable?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Concrete inputs and actions with an observable expected outcome.

recap: Describe a requirement in terms of people and outcomes.
Separate scope, assumptions, and implementation choices.
Write acceptance criteria for valid and invalid cases.
